findings.title: publish() metrics callback lets KeyError/ValueError escape into the execution memory-pressure hot path and abort a live job
findings.description: The `publish` closure installed as `ExecutionContext.memory_pressure_callback` wraps ONLY `store.require_job(job_id)` in `try/except Exception: return`. The two operations that run after the guard — `require_job_status(job)` (raises `ValueError` on a status not in `JOB_STATUSES`) and `store.atomic_update(job_id, {...}, expected_status=RUNNING_STATUS)` (raises `KeyError` when `job_id` is no longer present) — are OUTSIDE the try/except. `memory_pressure_callback(event)` is invoked unguarded from `ExecutionContext._record_memory_pressure_events` (`_execution_context.py:947-948`), which runs on the execution sampling path via `_observe_rss`. The `stage()` contextmanager only catches `ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError`, so a `KeyError`/`ValueError` raised here propagates up and aborts the running execution. The reachable trigger is a TOCTOU eviction/deletion: `require_job` succeeds, then the running job is evicted by TTL (`_evict_stale` for a stale running job, see `_job_store.py:106-111`) or removed via `delete_job`/`clear_result_data` on another thread, then `atomic_update` does `old = self._jobs[job_id]` (`_job_store.py:413`, documented `Raises KeyError if job_id does not exist`) and raises `KeyError`. A best-effort metrics publish thereby becomes a fatal execution failure. The `if status != RUNNING_STATUS: return` guard does not help because it runs before the window and does not prevent eviction of a running job.
findings.evidence:
_job_lifecycle.py: `try:
    job = store.require_job(job_id)
except Exception:
    return
status = require_job_status(job)  # ValueError escapes here
if status != RUNNING_STATUS:
    return
store.atomic_update(job_id, {...}, expected_status=RUNNING_STATUS)  # KeyError escapes if job evicted`. Callback invoked unguarded at _execution_context.py:947-948 `if self.memory_pressure_callback is not None: self.memory_pressure_callback(event)`, reached from _observe_rss -> _record_memory_pressure_events; stage() at _execution_context.py:726-728 only catches ExecutionMemoryLimitExceededError. atomic_update raises KeyError per _job_store.py:413 and its docstring.

findings.title: childNodeIds persisted in non-deterministic set order, diverging from the parser sibling path
findings.description: `child_node_ids = {n.id for n in child_nodes}` is a set comprehension. The set is correctly used for order-independent membership tests (e.g. `e.source in child_node_ids`), but it is then materialised three times via `list(child_node_ids)` — into the submodel placeholder node config, into `existing_submodels[sm_name]["childNodeIds"]`, and into the `SubmodelGraphResult`. CPython set iteration order is hash-seeded and not the graph node order, so the persisted `childNodeIds` lists are non-deterministic across processes/runs, producing churn in the saved `.haute.json` and the generated module for an otherwise identical create operation. The parse-time path that builds the same submodel metadata uses a deterministic, order-preserving list (`_parser_submodels.py:174` `child_node_ids = [n.id for n in sm_graph.nodes]`), so the two sibling builders — which `_submodel_graph.py`'s docstring says are meant to share submodel-construction logic — disagree on ordering. Behaviour is unaffected because downstream consumers treat the field as a set (`codegen.py:969` `set(sm_meta.get("childNodeIds", []))`, `projection.py:2224` `sorted(children)`), so this is a reproducibility/consistency defect, not a functional one. The fix is to derive an ordered list `[n.id for n in child_nodes]` for the materialisations while keeping a set for membership, matching the parser path.
findings.evidence: _submodel_ops.py:48 `child_node_ids = {n.id for n in child_nodes}` (set); lines 83/96/113 each emit `list(child_node_ids)`. Compare _parser_submodels.py:174 `child_node_ids = [n.id for n in sm_graph.nodes]` (ordered). Consumers are order-agnostic: codegen.py:969, projection.py:2224.

findings.title: Cancellation path silently swallows CancelledError and skips the structured failure log when the started worker raises after the request is cancelled
findings.description: In run_blocking_with_response_timeout's `except asyncio.CancelledError` branch, the drain loop `while not blocking_task.done(): await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` only catches asyncio.CancelledError (to re-loop on re-cancellation). If the already-started worker thread finishes by raising an ordinary (non-cancellation) exception, `await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` re-raises that worker exception. Because it is not an asyncio.CancelledError, it is not caught by the `except asyncio.CancelledError: continue` arm: it propagates out of the while loop AND out of the entire `except asyncio.CancelledError` block. Two consequences follow: (1) the trailing bare `raise` (which re-raises the original CancelledError) is never reached, so the in-flight request cancellation is suppressed and converted into a domain exception, violating the asyncio structured-concurrency contract that a coroutine catching CancelledError must re-raise it; upstream cancellation/limiters may then treat the task as 'failed' rather than 'cancelled'. (2) `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` is skipped, so the dedicated structured `route_work_background_failed` error log for a worker that failed after cancellation is never emitted (the failure is only visible as whatever exception type the caller did not expect). This contradicts the project's 'fail loudly / observable failures' principle. The normal-return cancellation path (worker returns a value) is correct and is the only behaviour the existing test test_run_blocking_with_response_timeout_cancellation_waits_for_worker exercises; the worker-raises-after-cancel branch is untested.
findings.evidence: Lines 51-58: `except asyncio.CancelledError:` then `while not blocking_task.done(): try: await asyncio.shield(blocking_task) except asyncio.CancelledError: continue` then `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` then `raise`. asyncio.shield's returned awaitable propagates the inner task's result/exception unless the OUTER await is cancelled; so a worker raising e.g. ValueError makes `await asyncio.shield(blocking_task)` raise ValueError, which the `except asyncio.CancelledError` arm does not catch -> escapes both the while loop and the outer except block, bypassing `_drain_background_future_result(blocking_task)` and the `raise`. Contrast the timeout branch (lines 47-50), which deliberately routes background failures through `blocking_task.add_done_callback(_drain_background_future_result)` so a late worker exception IS logged. The cancellation branch lacks that guarantee. The drain helper itself (lines 61-70) is the only place the `route_work_background_failed` structured error is produced.
